Summary # This sample is an old 2024 fake government app, actually built from a Chinese live-streaming codebase, and shipped in Virbox armor. This post unpacks it, walks through the RAT inside, and notes down everything I learned along the way.
SHA-256: e642a96d45f1e977d04463b267595da7228887c0db26529c7c4e6179476f8381
Info # First look # Before touching the DEX, I ran apkid. And there it was: Virbox Protector
What the manifest confesses # Package: com.phommvb.dotihanj # Permissions # 27 permissions, and the combo reads like a RAT shopping list.
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.REQUEST_DELETE_PACKAGES"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.GET_INSTALLED_APPS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.GRANT_RUNTIME_PERMISSIONS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_SYNC_STATS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_SYNC_SETTINGS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.DISABLE_KEYGUARD"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WAKE_LOCK"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WRITE_SETTINGS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_SMS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SEND_SMS"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_WIFI_STATE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SET_WALLPAPER"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CALL_PHONE"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BATTERY_STATS"/> Entry Point # v4ccd64a6.l4ccd64a6. This is the first code executed when the process is created, before any Activity. Its constructor hardcodes the protector’s identity as a logging tag: meta-data SAPP_NAME = "com.yiwuzhibo.BaseApplication" - a configuration value read by the loader at runtime naming the real Application class. <meta-data android:name="SAPP_NAME" android:value="com.yiwuzhibo.BaseApplication"/> com.yiwuzhibo.* the code inside is literally a Chinese livestreaming app
Accessibility # <service android:label="@string/ehv" android:name="com.yiwuzhibo.controller.TouchAccessibilityService" android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE" android:enabled="true" android:exported="true"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="android.accessibilityservice.AccessibilityService"/> </intent-filter> <meta-data android:name="android.accessibilityservice" android:resource="@xml/ao4"/> </service> The manifest asks Android to bind TouchAccessibilityService — and once the victim flips that switch, the app sees every screen its capabilities are defined in @xml/ao4:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <accessibility-service xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android" android:description="@string/r39" android:accessibilityEventTypes="typeAllMask" android:accessibilityFeedbackType="feedbackAllMask" android:notificationTimeout="10" android:accessibilityFlags="flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows|flagReportViewIds|flagRequestEnhancedWebAccessibility|flagIncludeNotImportantViews" android:canRetrieveWindowContent="true" android:canRequestEnhancedWebAccessibility="true" android:canPerformGestures="true"/> accessibilityEventTypes="typeAllMask" ← receives EVERY event type notificationTimeout="10" ← real-time, 10 ms delivery delay flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows ← inspects all open windows flagReportViewIds ← identifies exact input fields by view ID flagRequestEnhancedWebAccessibility ← can inject scripts into WebView content flagIncludeNotImportantViews ← nothing on screen is filtered out canRetrieveWindowContent="true" ← reads full on-screen content canPerformGestures="true" ← performs taps/swipes autonomously Persistence # Declaration Notes Permission RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED Wake on device start-up AutoRestart receiver — BOOT_COMPLETED intent-filter, exported="true" Relaunches malware components after every reboot Supporting: REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS, WAKE_LOCK, DISABLE_KEYGUARD Survives battery-saving kills; keeps CPU awake; can dismiss the keyguard Signing Certificate # Command: keytool -printcert -jarfile <sample>
Signer #1: Certificate #1: Owner: C=(1), ST=(1), L=(1), O=(1), OU=(1), CN=(1) ← literally "(1)" in every field Serial number: 0x42b84b3b Valid from: Sun Jun 25 13:46:40 ICT 2023 until: Thu Jun 18 13:46:40 ICT 2048 Certificate fingerprints: SHA1: 4C:BD:DC:EF:1D:FD:04:58:6B:76:40:2C:D0:46:82:8D:1D:D4:B7:A3 SHA256: 81:AB:77:80:79:AE:2A:36:D5:4E:D8:C9:C8:53:96:BF:CD:12:70:E4:4C:15:32:31:9D:65:B2:1E:33:82:25:A3 Signature algorithm: SHA256withRSA Subject Public Key Algorithm: 2048-bit RSA key Valid from 2023-06-25, ~6.5 months before the APK build timestamp (2024-01-11 from zip entries) → signing infrastructure prepared in advance of the campaign. Every DN field is the literal string (1) — an anonymous throwaway keystore. The SHA-256 above is a solid pivot indicator for sibling samples in this campaign. Deep Dive # The Virbox armor # Virbox Startup and Application Handoff # attachBaseContext it works like a TLS callback in Windows that is run first, before the entry point. It loads the native lib corresponding arch and calls the native initial function.
The Virbox wrapper’s overridden onCreate() prepares the runtime environment and then calls the original application’s onCreate() (com.yiwuzhibo.BaseApplication)
@Override public void onCreate() { if (this.f135d != null) { // The original Application was created. try { m4a(); // Replace framework references to the Virbox Application. m5b(); // Point resources and assets to the restored app. m7e(); // Restore and initialize content providers. } catch (Exception e) { e.printStackTrace(); } } super.onCreate(); // Call Android's base Application.onCreate(). Application application = this.f135d; if (application != null) { try { application.onCreate(); // Start the original application's initialization. } catch (Exception e2) { e2.printStackTrace(); } } } This malware uses string encryption throughout entire this class, this is the method string encryption:
public static String m3h(byte[] bArr) { for (int i = 0; i < bArr.length; i++) { bArr[i] = (byte) (bArr[i] ^ 105); } return new String(bArr, 0, bArr.length); } classes.dex # classes.dex is 5.130.552 bytes, but its declared DEX structures end at offset 17.224 ( 0x4348 ). The remaining 5.113.328 bytes from an appended Virbox-protected blob that begins with the VBPD marker.
So this is the APK structure once we decompress it.
APK ├─ classes.dex │ ├─ First 17KB: stub (wrapper v4ccd64a6 + jntm) ← unencrypted code │ └─ 5.11MB tail: "VBPD" blob ← ✗ PACKED: the entire real app lives here ├─ assets/l4ccd64a6_{a64,a32,x64,x86}.so ← GROUP A: Virbox loader (per-ABI) ├─ assets/kqkticwjgzy.dat (magic SENS) ← loader's auxiliary encrypted config ├─ lib/*/libnative-lib.so ← GROUP B: real app — NOT encrypted └─ lib/*/libstrategy.so ← GROUP B: strategies — NOT encrypted libstrategy.so — Embedded PIN-Harvesting Strategies # The library exposes two JNI entry points consumed by the packed DEX layer: Java_com_yiwuzhibo_utils_StrangeFactory_getStrategyData and Java_com_yiwuzhibo_utils_StrangeFactory_getPhoneData. Embedded in .rodata are 19 JSON configuration objects that instruct the accessibility service what to read on which screen.
config schema (two families):
Field Meaning condition.pkg / nodes foreground package + view IDs that trigger the strategy listens.listenMethod capture mode: listenClick (keypad node→digit map), listenTextPassword (read password field), listenMask, listenChild (pattern view) listens.keys view-ID → digit mapping for keypad reconstruction listens.returnType capture payload: text / image / video (screen recording for pattern locks) useIn.brand / ui / uiVersion device OEM / launcher skin the entry applies to Representative entry (Samsung One UI lockscreen PIN):
{"strategyName": "samsung keys", "strategyType": "pin", "useIn": {"brand": "samsung", "ui": "One UI"}, "condition": {"pkg": "com.android.systemui", "nodes": ["com.android.systemui:id/pinEntry"]}, "listens": {"listenMethod": "listenClick", "returnType": "text", "keys": {"com.android.systemui:id/key1": "1", "com.android.systemui:id/key0": "0", "com.android.systemui:id/delete_button": "-1"}, "keyIsFloat": false}} Covered targets: The embedded strategy
Target Package Note Device lockscreen PIN/pattern com.android.systemui Samsung, Xiaomi, Vivo, OPPO, Realme, OnePlus, Motorola, Meizu, Infinix, Honor VietinBank iPay 🇻🇳 com.vietinbank.ipay keypad ids tvmot…tvzero (Vietnamese numerals) mymo / GSB 🇹🇭 com.mobilife.gsb.mymo t9_key_1…0 Bangkok Bank 🇹🇭 com.bbl.mobilebanking number1…0 CIMB THAI 🇹🇭 com.cimbthai.digital.mycimb editTextPasscode TMB (ttb) 🇹🇭 com.TMBTOUCH.PRODUCTION grid_pad SCB EASY 🇹🇭 com.scb.phone button_1… Krungthai NEXT 🇹🇭 ktbcs.netbank btn1… The 19 embedded strategies serve a single purpose: harvesting unlock credentials - device lockscreen PIN/pattern and banking-app PINs. Coverage spans 10 OEM lockscreen skins and seven Southeast Asia banking apps: one Vietnamese and six Thai. Although this app shows many Vietnam-targeting characteristics, its embedded configurations still include numerous Thai banking apps. This suggests the malware was reused from another campaign targeting the APAC region. Full strategy : link
Unpacking Virbox # Dynamic Unpacking # Run it on a rooted phone and the Virbox loader kills itself by jumping to 0xdead3000 — anti-analysis.
adb logcat -d -b crash 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : signal 11 (SIGSEGV), code 1 (SEGV_MAPERR), fault addr 0x00000000dead3000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x0 00000000dead3000 x1 0000000000000000 x2 0000000000000000 x3 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x4 0000000000000000 x5 0000000000000000 x6 0000000000000000 x7 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x8 0000000000000000 x9 0000000000000000 x10 0000000000000000 x11 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x12 0000000000000000 x13 0000000000000000 x14 0000000000000000 x15 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x16 0000000000000000 x17 0000000000000000 x18 0000000000000000 x19 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x20 0000000000000000 x21 0000000000000000 x22 0000000000000000 x23 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x24 0000000000000000 x25 0000000000000000 x26 0000000000000000 x27 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : x28 0000000000000000 x29 0000000000000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : lr 0000007a988981d4 sp 0000000000000000 pc 00000000dead3000 pst 0000000060000000 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : #00 pc 00000000dead3000 <unknown> 11-04 08:49:38.621 19310 19310 F DEBUG : #01 pc 00000000002381d0 /data/data/com.phommvb.dotihanj/files/.ss/l4ccd64a6.so To deal with this, we just need to add com.phommvb.dotihanj into Magisk’s denylist.
adb shell su magisk --denylist add com.phommvb.dotihanj magisk --denylist enable magisk --denylist status Now I’m in
As we know, there are 2 encrypted DEX files in the tail of classes.dex. Virbox has to decrypt both at runtime to feed them to ART.
Virbox (l4ccd64a6.so) decrypts the DEX in memory ↓ DexFile / InMemoryDexClassLoader / direct native call ↓ ART: libdexfile.so → DexFileLoader::Open(buffer, size, ...) ↓ ← OUR HOOK SITS HERE — the bytes exist intact, plaintext, at that exact moment We could hook Java APIs (like DexClassLoader,…) can be bypassed by packer; hooking libdexfile.so cannot be avoided by anyone - it is the deepest layer every DEX must show up there.
// one job: dump every DEX ART ingests. frida -U -f com.phommvb.dotihanj -l dump-dex-mini.js //frida -U -f com.phommvb.dotihanj -l dump-dex-mini.js //adb shell su -c "cp /data/data/com.phommvb.dotihanj/dump-*.dex /sdcard/Download/" //adb pull /sdcard/Download const fopen = new NativeFunction(Module.getGlobalExportByName("fopen"), "pointer", ["pointer", "pointer"]); const fwrite = new NativeFunction(Module.getGlobalExportByName("fwrite"), "size_t", ["pointer", "size_t", "size_t", "pointer"]); const fclose = new NativeFunction(Module.getGlobalExportByName("fclose"), "int", ["pointer"]); const wb = Memory.allocUtf8String("wb"); const seen = new Set(); let n = 0; function dump(p) { try { const m = p.readU32(); // "dex\n" or "cdex" if (m !== 0x0a786564 && m !== 0x78656463) return; const size = p.add(0x20).readU32(); // header file_size if (size < 0x70 || seen.has(p.toString())) return; p.add(size - 1).readU8(); // readable to the end? seen.add(p.toString()); const f = fopen(Memory.allocUtf8String("/data/data/com.phommvb.dotihanj/dump-" + ++n + ".dex"), wb); if (f.isNull()) return; fwrite(p, 1, size, f); fclose(f); console.log("[dump] #" + n + " " + size + " bytes @ " + p); } catch (_) {} } //Step 1 : Gets the libdexfile.so module and enumberates all its symbols for (const s of Process.findModuleByName("libdexfile.so").enumerateSymbols()) { //Open: The real ingestion //IsMagicValid if (s.type === "function" && /DexFileLoader.*(Open|IsMagicValid)/.test(s.name)) Interceptor.attach(s.address, { onEnter(a) { for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) dump(a[i]); } }); } Now we dumped out 5 DEX files
# What it was 1 APK’s stub classes.dex 2 Payload DEX #1 (9.6 MB, via Open) 3 com/fakeClass 316-byte decoy, address A 4 Payload DEX #2 (2.6 MB, via Open) 5 Same 316-byte decoy, address B (.ss/classes2.dex) Static Unpacking # Find the native parser # This snippet (in ARM64 .so) checks for the Virbox blob signature, VBPD. Along this execution path, the obfuscating arithmetic operations cancel out, while temporary values are overwritten before the final comparison.
So the simplified code is:
0x060FB0 LDR W8, [X25] 0x060FE4 MOV W9, #0x4256 0x061018 MOVK W9, #0x4450, LSL #16 0x061060 CMP W8, W9 So X25 is the start address of packed Virbox blob. Now, we have to trace which function call this method to check signature. If it matches, the flow will jump to 0x59C10
Starting at 0x59C10 and following the code forward, we reach an indirect branch, BR X17, at 0x59D1C
After all, X17 is equal 0xC0FE0 , instruction:
0x59C40 LDR W0, qword_59C90 ; Read 0x0006739E ; LDR = Load Register 0x59C54 SXTW X0, W0 ; X0 = 0x6739E ; SXTW = Sign Extend Word 0x59C70 ADR X1, qword_59C90 ; X1 = 0x59C90 ; ADR = Address generation relative to the current instruction 0x59C8C B loc_59C9C ; Skip embedded data and 0x59C98 ; B = jmp ; Literal at 0x59C90: ; 9E 73 06 00 → 0x0006739E 0x59C9C ADD X0, X0, X1 ; X0 = 0xC102E 0x59CB0 STR X0, [SP,#0x18] ; Save target precursor,Mem64[P + 0x18] = 0xC102E ;STR = Store 0x59CC4 LDP X0, X1, [SP],#0x10 ; SP advances by 0x10 ; LDP = Load Pair of Registers. 0x59CE0 LDR X17, [SP,#8] ; Reload saved value: X17 = 0xC102E 0x59CFC ADD SP, SP, #0x10 ; Stack cleanup 0x59D00 AND X17, X17, X17 ; X17 unchanged 0x59D04 SUB X17, X17, #0x44 ; X17 = 0xC0FEA 0x59D08 SUB SP, SP, #0xD0 0x59D0C ADD SP, SP, #0x40 0x59D10 ADD SP, SP, #0x90 ; These three SP changes cancel 0x59D14 SUB X17, X17, #0xA ; X17 = 0xC0FE0 0x59D18 ADD X17, X17, #0 ; X17 unchanged 0x59D1C BR X17 ; Jump to 0xC0FE0 Continue with 0xC0FE0, the program will jump into 0x1F23F8:
Keep going keep going, we will catch:
0x1F2874 B loc_25C098 Did you remember X25, yeah it’s the head of Virbox blob. This instruction loads 16 bytes from VBPD + 0x28 into Q0. Then jump to 0x62AE0
Keep Going we catch an BR again 0x62BF8 BR X19. If you trace X19:
0x62B28 LDR W0, off_62B64 ; Read bytes 4A 1F 1A 00. ; W0 = 0x001A1F4A. 0x62B3C SXTW X0, W0 ; Sign-extend the 32-bit value. ; X0 = 0x1A1F4A. 0x62B58 ADR X1, off_62B64 ; X1 = address of the literal = 0x62B64. 0x62B60 B loc_62B70 ; Skip the embedded literal and intervening instructions. 0x62B70 ADD X0, X0, X1 ; X0 = 0x1A1F4A + 0x62B64 = 0x204AAE. 0x62B84 STR X0, [SP,#0x18] ; Save 0x204AAE. ; Let the current SP be P: store at P + 0x18. 0x62B98 LDP X0, X1, [SP],#0x10 ; Load the saved register pair, then SP = P + 0x10. 0x62BB4 LDR X19, [SP,#8] ; Read from P + 0x10 + 8 = P + 0x18. ; X19 = 0x204AAE. 0x62BD0 ADD SP, SP, #0x10 0x62BD4 STP X19, X30, [SP,#-0x10]! ; Save the current X19 and X30. 0x62BD8 LDR X19, loc_62BD8 ; Temporarily overwrite X19. 0x62BDC LDP X19, X30, [SP],#0x10 ; Restore the saved X19 = 0x204AAE. 0x62BE0 SUB X19, X19, #0x44 ; X19 = 0x204A6A. 0x62BE4 B loc_62BE8 0x62BE8 SUB X19, X19, #0x22 ; X19 = 0x204A48. 0x62BEC STP X19, X30, [SP,#-0x10]! ; Save X19 = 0x204A48. 0x62BF0 LDR X19, loc_62BF0 ; Temporarily overwrite X19 again. 0x62BF4 LDP X19, X30, [SP],#0x10 ; Restore X19 = 0x204A48. 0x62BF8 BR X19 ; Continue execution at 0x204A48. Keep going, we almost there from 0x204A48.We got:
0x204A6C B loc_18B530 and then:
0x18B58C B loc_25C0A8 at 0x25C0A8 we got:
0x25C0A8 MOVI V1.16B, #0x2A 0x25C0AC EOR V0.16B, V0.16B, V1.16B Q0 and V0.16B refer to the same 128-bit register, viewed using different notation. Two instructions above mean:
#Move it copies the constant 0x2A into every byte of V1 V1 = [2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A 2A] ## EOR destination, source1, source2 = XOR for i in range(16): v0[i] = v0[i] ^ v1[i] ## It mean the program will XOR the first 16-bytes from VBPD + 0x28 Keep tracking, we will get:
171D78 BR X3 ;X3 = 0x188528 And then:
192DBC B loc_25C0E8 At 25C0E8:
.text:000000000025C0E8 STUR Q0, [X29,#-0x70] .text:000000000025C0EC B word_1FCC08 STUR instruction stores the XORed value into [X29-0x70], and if you notice, we just skimmed past
.text:0000000000192B14 SUB X1, X29, #0x70 ; 'p' It means The XORed value is stored into X1 And then… a dozen obfuscated trampolines later (0x1FCC08 → 0xd8308 → 0x1196EC → … → 0x25FD50), we finally hit a real instruction:
0x25FD50 LDR Q0, [X12, #0xDE0] Inspect the bytes being loaded
X12 = 0x2B2000 X12 + 0xDE0 = 0x2B2DE0 If you check the source bytes at 0x2B2DE0:
00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F So Q0 receives the numbers 0 through 15
Virbox payload structure and offline unpacking # 1. Locate the protected container # The original classes.dex contains a VBPD container starting at file offset 0x4348, immediately after the wrapper’s declared DEX data section. The container occupies 0x4E05F0 bytes. The native VBPD signature check provided an analysis anchor. Offline ARM64 emulation exposed the key preparation and buffer transformations through the obfuscated control flow.
2. VBPD header # Offsets below are relative to the beginning of VBPD. Integer fields use little-endian encoding.
Offset Size Field Value 0x00 4 bytes Signature VBPD 0x04–0x17 20 bytes Additional protector metadata 0x49D6, 0, 0, 1, 2 0x18 4 bytes Main ciphertext length 0x4DEDD2 0x1C 4 bytes Main decompressed length 0xBAE530 0x20 4 bytes Auxiliary ciphertext length 0x17E6 0x24 4 bytes Auxiliary decompressed length 0x1868 0x28 16 bytes Encoded RC4 key See below 0x38 Variable Main ciphertext, followed by auxiliary ciphertext Two sections The meanings of the additional metadata fields were unnecessary for extraction.
3. RC4 key derivation # The 16 bytes stored at VBPD + 0x28, corresponding to classes.dex + 0x4370, are:
02 7C 4C 55 AB D5 40 76 41 DF 4C 8A 9D 72 CA 02 The loader XORs each byte with 0x2A:
key = bytes(value ^ 0x2A for value in blob[0x28:0x38]) The resulting RC4 key is:
28 56 66 7F 81 FF 6A 5C 6B F5 66 A0 B7 58 E0 28 2856667f81ff6a5c6bf566a0b758e028 The native routines were identified as:
0x25FD24: RC4 state initialization and key scheduling. 0x25FE68: RC4 keystream generation and input XOR. Identification was supported by the 256-entry permutation, index updates, swaps, and XOR loop. An independent implementation matched the native key-scheduling state and the first 256 transformed bytes. 4. Encrypted sections # Ranges below exclude the ending offset.
Section Range within VBPD Range within original classes.dex Encrypted size Main [0x38, 0x4DEE0A) [0x4380, 0x4E3152) 5,107,154 bytes Auxiliary [0x4DEE0A, 0x4E05F0) [0x4E3152, 0x4E4938) 6,118 bytes The loader initializes RC4 once, decrypts the main section, and then continues decrypting the auxiliary section using the same evolving state. Core extraction logic: cipher = RC4(key) main_frame = cipher.update(blob[0x38:0x4DEE0A]) aux_frame = cipher.update(blob[0x4DEE0A:0x4E05F0]) main = zstd_decompress(main_frame) aux = zstd_decompress(aux_frame) Both decrypted sections begin with Zstandard magic 28 B5 2F FD. Their decompressed lengths match the header:
Main: 0xBAE530 bytes — two consecutive DEX files. Auxiliary: 0x1868 bytes — metadata and separately encrypted method records. 5. Recover DEX files and protected methods # The main plaintext contains:
File Offset within main plaintext Size Classes classes.dex 0x000000 0x933260 bytes 8,190 classes2.dex 0x933260 0x27B2D0 bytes 2,557 Both extracted DEX files pass their embedded SHA-1 and Adler-32 checks. The auxiliary plaintext contains 46 encrypted method records. Each record carries its own raw 16-byte RC4 key and stored length. A fresh RC4 state decrypts each record, revealing a dvmp header, an original DEX method index, and a standard Dalvik code_item. The recovered method bodies were restored, and dexlib2 rebuilt canonical DEX layouts. Result: two analysis DEX files containing 10,747 classes, with 46 protected method bodies restored. Native string encryption remains unresolved. Inside the dropped DEX # The recovered application combines a Vietnamese public-service registration/login lure with a remote command service. This build is tailored for Vietnam and uses the vietDichVuCong build flavor.
How the DEX files fit together # Component DEX Role BaseApplication, SplashActivity, DichRegister*Activity First Application startup and public-service lure WantCommonService, RemoteCommandClient First Command connection, dispatch, reporting, plugin relay TouchAccessibilityService, AutoClick, action classes First UI observation, gestures, overlays, settings automation PasswordCapture2, BankCapture, StrategyFactory First Bank/lockscreen strategy consumers, with channel-dependent gates k1.a / k1.f First Retrofit API definition and HTTP client LoginVM, Command, DeviceInfo, other models Second Submission logic and cross-component payloads AutoRestart, GlobalBroadcast Second Boot restart and local command effects DisplayService, ScreenRecordService, VideoRecorder Second Streaming/recording implementations r4.e, r4.h, r4.o0 Second Preferences, flavor gates, SMS collection Agora implementation Second Bundled media SDK; use is constrained by the flavor gates Decoding the strings # Both DEX files’ strings are decoded by a native function m4ccd64a6.F4ccd64a6_11
All strings are obfuscated with this algorithm:
"<_3C31332E3E36316C7879363D387D44404D4139" ││└────────────────────────────────────── Hex-encoded bytes │└─────────────────────────────────────── XOR key: '_' = 0x5F └──────────────────────────────────────── Unused by this decoding formula So, how do we clean up this mess? Thankfully, Jadx has a Jadx Script (Kotlin) plugin to run a custom string decryption script. The script replaces calls to m4ccd64a6.F4ccd64a6_11 that have constant string arguments with their decoded values directly in decompiled view. The code above becomes:
Malicious Behaviors # SMS collection and sending # Inbox upload — command 57 requests READ_SMS when missing, then collects:
WantCommonService.onReceiverCommand -> r4.o0.a -> r4.o0$a.invoke (query) -> r4.o0$b.invoke -> k1.a.g -> POST x/common-sms r4.o0$a queries content://sms/inbox for columns address, date, body with the selection string " date DESC limit 50" — the 50 most recent messages — and wraps each row in a MessageInfo(address, body, date). The list is POSTed as JSON to x/common-sms.
C2 Communication # Address (defanged) Role https://app[.]vnac6[.]xyz HTTP API base — BuildConfig.BaseAddress, fed to Retrofit via reflection; stored token added as header ws://app[.]vnac6[.]xyz/x/command?token=<token>&width=<w>&height=<h> Default command channel — API host with scheme swapped to ws:// (plaintext WebSocket) ws://8[.]219[.]85[.]91:8888/push-streaming?id=1234 Stored video-push default (config lead; startup wiring incomplete, see Streaming) rtmp://101[.]37[.]81[.]24/test Separate PREF_RTMP_URL default (use not established) Session: WantCommonService.onCreate() builds RemoteCommandClient(this, listener) and calls startConnect(). On onOpen the client sends a DeviceInfo JSON fingerprint; the field named imei is populated from android_id via r4.n.b() (Settings.System.getString(..., "android_id")) — no hardware IMEI is proven. Protocol: messages parse as Command(action: String, uid: Int?, data: JsonElement?) → CommandHandler.onReceiverCommand() → the main dispatcher; heartbeat replies with action "0", the supplied uid, and an empty Data. Reconnect is scheduled 5 s after drops; the service polls permission status every 5 s and display dimensions every 2 s while connected. Secondary paths: EventBus (LiveEventBus) forwards between service and accessibility service; sendReplyMsg() relays serialized commands cross-application over fromMainData/ fromPluginData — the receiving application is outside the recovered DEX files. HTTP API surface (all under the base above): x/login, x/ad-login, x/user-extra, x/user-edit, x/user-bank-pwd, x/common-sms, x/common-app, x/common-upload (multipart), x/common-log, x/ws-log, x/common-bank-list, x/bank-rule-list, x/command-report. The network security config permits cleartext and trusts user CAs; the command channel is plaintext WebSocket by default. Command 99 can replace streaming configuration at runtime.
